Midas cichlid (Amphilophus citrinellus) reaches a maximum total body length of 28.7 centimeters [Li = 28.7 centimeters] among males, a size attained only after several years of continuous somatic growth in the productive lakes of its native Nicaraguan range. Large males are competitively dominant in nesting territories, and this ultimate size enables them to defend spawning sites effectively against conspecifics. Field surveys across Lake Managua have documented that male Midas cichlids typically surpass 24 centimeters in standard length, with the largest individuals exceeding the sample maximum recorded in museum collections. The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in size, as females seldom reach the same formidable dimensions, rarely exceeding 20 centimeters in total length. This pattern aligns with the social system observed in many substrate-brooding neotropical cichlids, where male competition for spawning territories imposes strong selective pressure toward large body size. The growth trajectory follows an asymptotic curve typical of iteroparous teleosts, with the most rapid gains occurring during the first two years before the rate tapers considerably as the fish approach their asymptotic length.

Puberty in this species is reached at a total length of 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal differentiation and the capacity to participate in spawning aggregations. Individuals below this length rarely exhibit mature gonadal tissue, and histological examination of wild-caught specimens reveals that vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis commence abruptly once this somatic benchmark is achieved. The comparatively modest size at sexual maturation reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction in an environment where adult mortality can be high due to predation pressure from larger piscivores. Breeding activity peaks during the rainy season, when water levels rise and newly flooded littoral zones provide abundant nesting substrate and cover for fry. Reproductively active males develop a pronounced nuchal hump, a secondary sexual characteristic that becomes evident shortly after the pubertal length is attained. The timing of first spawning relative to this pubertal milestone depends on social conditions, as dominant individuals typically secure territories before subordinate males initiate reproductive efforts.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge after an incubation period of approximately three to four days under optimal thermal conditions. At the moment of hatching, each prolarva carries a substantial yolk reserve that sustains it through the first days of development. The wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams], a mass that reflects the energy invested per offspring in a species producing relatively small but numerous ova. Egg diameter in Amphilophus citrinellus averages near 1.5 millimeters, consistent with the maternal investment strategy common among Central American cichlids that guard their broods extensively. Following yolk absorption, the exotrophic transition occurs when the mouth opens and the free-swimming larva begins exogenous feeding on microzooplankton. The newly feeding fry grow rapidly, channeling most assimilated energy into somatic tissue rather than storage, which is typical of cichlid larvae inhabiting productive tropical waters. Mortality during the first weeks is substantial, with estimates suggesting that fewer than five percent of hatched larvae survive to the juvenile stage in the wild.

Females produce clutches ranging from 300 to 1000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 300 to 1000 eggs per spawning event], a fecundity that scales positively with maternal body size. Under the thermal regime characteristic of Lake Managua during the breeding season, approximately 24 °C [T = 24 °C], individual females typically spawn one clutch every 60 days [F_R_i = one clutch every 60 days], maintaining this frequency throughout the extended reproductive period. This spawning interval reflects the time required for ovarian recrudescence, courtship, egg deposition, and biparental brood care, during which both parents fan and defend the adhesive eggs until hatching. Clutch size is influenced by female condition, as individuals with greater lipid reserves produce larger clutches. The combination of moderate fecundity per event and relatively frequent spawning across the breeding season allows females to achieve considerable lifetime reproductive output, even in the face of high early life mortality. Parental care continues for several weeks after hatching, with both adults guarding the free-swimming school of fry and leading them to foraging areas.

The species attains a maximum recorded adult wet weight of 747.5 grams [Wwi = 747.5 grams], a figure derived from the length–weight relationship established for populations in Lake Managua. This ultimate body mass is among the largest documented within the genus Amphilophus, whose members are renowned for their trophic diversification across the Nicaraguan lake system. The longevity of this cichlid reaches approximately nine years [am = approximately nine years] when maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] in captive settings, with wild individuals likely experiencing somewhat shorter lifespans due to predation, disease, and the energetic costs of repeated spawning. Senescent individuals show declining condition factors and reduced gonadal output before death. The relatively long lifespan combined with iteroparous reproduction positions Midas cichlid as a moderate-paced life-history strategist among neotropical cichlids, contrasting with smaller annual species in the same family. Field mark–recapture studies indicate that survival rates remain high through the middle adult years before declining sharply after age seven, consistent with actuarial senescence in long-lived teleosts.
